title: Let Weighty Decisions Marinate While You Focus on Other Matters
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article explores how the brain continues processing a decision unconsciously even after conscious attention shifts elsewhere, and argues leaders should deliberately harness that background processing. The technique involves clearly articulating a problem statement in writing, mentally priming the brain to work on it, and then setting it aside rather than forcing continuous analysis. Research cited in the piece suggests decisions made after a period of distraction or sleep tend to be higher quality than those reached through pure uninterrupted analysis. The author closes by noting that famous creative epiphanies often result from this same priming process, even when the thinkers themselves don't credit it explicitly.
points: The brain continues processing a decision unconsciously even when conscious attention moves elsewhere
Research suggests decisions made after distraction or sleep tend to be higher quality than pure continuous analysis
The technique: write a clear problem statement, mentally prime the brain, then deliberately set it aside
Famous creative epiphanies often result from this same priming process, even when unacknowledged
quotes: Even when leaders are not actively trying to think through the decision or solve a problem, the brain continues processing it unconsciously in the background.
Research shows that the quality of decisions made after distraction, sleep, or inactivity is generally higher than those made by analysis without the benefit of downtime.

The first step to incorporate this marination process is to clearly identify the decision, problem, or opportunity you want the brain to work on. Articulating the problem statement in writing is essential.
If the decision is far out on the horizon, then occasionally repriming the brain by re-reading the statement can encourage the brain to keep the background analysis going.
Some of the world’s greatest thinkers, scientists, and artists describe these epiphanies in a host of books and manuscripts.
